title: LinkedIn Automation Limits: How to Pace Your Outreach Safely
summary: LinkedIn doesn't publish exact limits. Commonly cited ranges, a conservative ramp schedule, warning signs, and what to do if you get restricted.
body_markdown:
Everyone wants to know the number. How many connection requests can you send before LinkedIn shuts you down? The honest answer is that nobody outside LinkedIn knows, and the real limit depends on your account. This guide gives you the ranges people commonly cite, the factors that move them, and a conservative way to pace your outreach so one account problem doesn't stall your pipeline.


## First, the part most guides skip


LinkedIn's User Agreement prohibits using bots and other automated methods to access the service, send messages, or add contacts. Any tool that automates actions on your account, including ours, operates against those terms.


That doesn't mean every automated action gets flagged. It means you carry the risk. If LinkedIn restricts or bans your account, that's your account and your network. Go in knowingly, keep volumes low, and never automate an account you couldn't afford to lose.


## What LinkedIn actually publishes (and doesn't)


LinkedIn confirms that limits exist. Its help pages mention a weekly cap on invitations and say accounts can be restricted for sending too many invites or for activity that looks automated. It does not publish the exact numbers, and they appear to vary by account.


Everything below is a community rule of thumb, pieced together from what outbound teams report. Treat these as starting points, not safe zones.


### Commonly cited ranges


Action Commonly cited range A conservative cap to start


Connection requests Roughly 100 to 200 per week, depending on account age and standing 10 to 15 per day, under 80 per week


Messages to 1st-degree connections Often cited as 50 to 150 per day 20 to 40 per day


Profile views Often cited as 80 to 250 per day (higher on paid plans) 30 to 60 per day


Post likes Rarely discussed as a hard limit, but bursts look robotic 10 to 20 per day


Pending (unanswered) invites Problems often reported once this climbs into the high hundreds Keep it under 300 to 400


The conservative column sits well below the ranges on purpose. Nobody gets restricted for sending too few invites.


Free accounts also have a monthly cap on connection requests that include a personalized note, at the time of writing. If notes are central to your approach, check what your plan allows before building a sequence around them.


## The factors that seem to matter


LinkedIn's systems almost certainly look at more than a raw count. These are the factors outbound teams consistently report as moving the needle.


**Account age and history.** A two-year-old account with 800 connections and regular activity can usually do more than a three-week-old account with 40 connections. New accounts get the least slack.


**Acceptance rate.** If most people ignore or decline your requests, that's a signal you're spamming. A common rule of thumb is to watch for acceptance dropping below about 25 to 30 percent and treat that as a reason to slow down and fix targeting or copy.


**Pending invites.** A large pile of unanswered invites looks like spray-and-pray. It's one of the most common triggers people report, and it's the easiest one to fix (more on that below).


**"I don't know this person" reports.** When recipients click that, it counts against you. Better targeting reduces this more than any pacing setting.


**Activity outside of outreach.** Accounts that post, comment, and use LinkedIn like a normal person seem to get more room. Some teams use LinkedIn's Social Selling Index (SSI) as a rough health gauge. There's no public evidence that SSI sets your limits, but a higher score usually reflects the kind of normal activity that helps.


**Sudden spikes.** Going from 5 invites a day to 50 overnight is one of the clearest ways to get flagged. Consistency matters more than the number itself.


## A conservative ramp schedule


Use this as a starting template. "New" means under roughly six months old or fewer than a few hundred connections. "Established" means an older account with a real network and normal activity.


Week New account: invites/day New account: messages/day Established: invites/day Established: messages/day


1 5 10 10 20


2 8 15 15 30


3 10 20 20 40


4 and on 10 to 15 20 to 30 20 to 25 40 to 50


Two rules for moving up a row:


1. Only increase if acceptance rate is holding steady and you've seen no warnings that week.
2. If anything looks off, drop back a row and stay there for at least a week.


Keep weekly invites under roughly 100 even at the top of the established column, unless your account has a long, clean history and you're comfortable with the risk.


### Pace it like a human


Daily caps are only half of it. How the actions are spread out matters too.


- **Working hours only.** Run actions during business hours in your own time zone, roughly 8am to 6pm. A burst of 40 invites at 3am is a pattern no human produces.
- **Randomized gaps.** Spread actions across the day with irregular spacing, not one every 60 seconds on the dot.
- **Weekdays, with lighter weekends.** Many teams pause entirely on weekends or run at a fraction of weekday volume.
- **Mix the actions.** Profile visit, then a post like a day or two later, then the connection request. That looks like interest, not a script.


## Warning signs to watch for


Stop and reassess immediately if you see any of these:


- A message saying you've reached the weekly invitation limit
- Security checks or CAPTCHAs appearing more often than usual
- A prompt asking you to verify your identity
- Being logged out repeatedly or asked to re-enter your password
- A notice that your account is temporarily restricted
- A sudden drop in acceptance rate or profile views


The weekly limit message usually just means you're done for the week. The others suggest LinkedIn is looking more closely.


## What to do if you get restricted


1. **Pause all automation on that account right away.** Don't try to push through or switch tools.
2. **Follow LinkedIn's own steps.** If it asks for ID verification, complete it through LinkedIn directly. Don't hand credentials or ID documents to anyone who offers to restore your account for you.
3. **Wait it out.** Temporary restrictions are often reported to lift within a day to a couple of weeks. Use LinkedIn manually and lightly in the meantime.
4. **Restart at half your previous volume or lower.** Go back to the week 1 or week 2 row of the ramp table and climb slowly.
5. **Fix the cause.** Check pending invites, acceptance rate, and targeting. If you restart with the same list and copy, you'll likely end up in the same place.


## Clean up old pending invites


This is the single most useful maintenance habit. Go to My Network, open Manage invitations, select Sent, and withdraw invites that have sat unanswered for more than two to three weeks.


A few notes:


- Do it in small batches, not hundreds at once. Mass withdrawals can look automated too.
- LinkedIn's help pages say that after you withdraw an invite, you can't re-invite that same person for up to three weeks.
- Make it a weekly or biweekly routine so the pile never gets large.


If someone hasn't accepted in three weeks, try email instead.


## Let email carry the volume


The safest way to stay under LinkedIn limits is to not need much LinkedIn volume in the first place. Email can handle far more sends per day with a properly set-up domain and inboxes, while LinkedIn works best as a lighter touch alongside it.


A simple pattern: email first, then a profile visit, then a connection request only to contacts who opened or clicked but didn't reply. That keeps LinkedIn actions focused on people who've shown some interest, which tends to help acceptance rates and keeps daily volume low. ## The short version


- LinkedIn doesn't publish exact limits. The commonly cited range for connection requests is roughly 100 to 200 per week, and yours depends on your account.
- Automating LinkedIn goes against its User Agreement. Accept that risk knowingly and keep volumes conservative.
- Start low (5 to 10 invites a day), ramp slowly, run during working hours, and avoid sudden spikes.
- Watch acceptance rate and pending invites, and withdraw old invites every week or two.
- Let email carry most of your volume so LinkedIn can stay light.
